notes: \cpara{Lists Einfeld's honours. They match the Wikipedia article the post links: born 1938, Queen's Counsel in 1977, Australian Living Treasure in 1997, United Nations Peace Award in 2002, inaugural president of the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission (1986 to 1989), retired from the Federal Court in 2001. I could not confirm that he was ``routinely brought back to judge important cases.''}

\cpara{The ticket details match the linked article: A\$77, for 10 km/h (6.2 mph) over the limit, in 2006. To contest it he named as the driver a woman who, a journalist found, had died years before. He was sentenced in March 2009 to three years with a non-parole period of two, and served two.}

\cfact{``Started with'' fits what was public in April 2009. In July 2009, after the post, the New South Wales Bar Association put evidence to the Court of Appeal that he had also named absent academics as drivers of his car in 1999 and 2003 (\textsc{Sydney Morning Herald}, 23 July 2009). Wikipedia reports that the court found these and a 2004 declaration proven; I could not read the judgment. These declarations seem to have come to light only after the 2006 case.}

\cpara{The post's point, with its own two caveats: the theory sounds ``suspiciously virtuous,'' and we hear of this case through ``obvious selective reporting.'' Both caveats are fair, and together they limit what the case can show: that lies sometimes blow up, which ``Entangled Truths, Contagious Lies'' (15 October 2008) had already granted, not how often.}

\clogic{The case fits the ``entangled traces'' part of the theory well. To defend one false name, Einfeld invented a second Teresa Brennan and produced a 20-page statement about her, the basis of his conviction for attempting to pervert the course of justice. It fits the ``honest people'' part less well, given the earlier false declarations reported after the post.}
